claims.text: The precursor is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr blend of metallic and hydride powders, specifically TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, and ZrH2.
The high-surface-area precursor is oxygen-affine and prone to forming HfO2.
A reactive elemental Ti getter under high vacuum will enable complete dehydrogenation of the precursor hydrides.
The Ti getter will reduce residual oxygen below 0.8 wt%.
A fast ramp to approximately 1300°C facilitates decomposition of the hydride blend.
Quenching at more than 100°C/s from approximately 1300°C will retain a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure.
Ti preferentially scavenges oxygen by forming TiO or TiO2 instead of allowing oxygen dissolution or HfO2 formation.
Hydride decomposition releases hydrogen and creates reactive surfaces.
An oxygen concentration of 0.8 wt% is a critical threshold for hardening and oxide precipitation in HfNbTaTiZr.
Dissolved oxygen stabilizes alpha-HCP nucleation in this equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr system.
Rapid quenching prevents diffusion-limited decomposition of beta-BCC into alpha-BCC plus beta-BCC.
The proposed regime will produce a relative density above 99%.
The quenched material will be single-phase BCC with no detectable alpha-BCC or alpha-HCP.
The quenched microstructure will have a sub-micron to few-micron grain size.
TiO precipitates will be the only oxide phase in the final material.
Sintering without adequate oxygen scavenging produces monoclinic HfO2 and significant oxygen-related hardening.
Inadequate oxygen scavenging causes alpha-HCP or alpha-BCC precipitation during cooling and degrades ductility.
Successful suppression of alpha phases requires a stoichiometric excess of Ti relative to the total oxygen inventory and a quench that bypasses the alpha-transformation nose.
The critical hydride-decomposition window for this blend is approximately 400–800°C.

contradictions.description: The mediator permits both TiO and TiO2 precipitates, whereas the predicted outcome states that TiO will be the only oxide phase.

The hypothesis calls the treatment a dual-stage sintering regime, but the specified intervention and conditions describe only a fast ramp to 1300°C followed by quenching, without defining two distinct stages or their holds.
